references.text: Satan presents himself before the Lord and asks for permission to test Job, just as he here asks to sift the disciples like wheat. In both cases, Satan must ask God for permission before he can attack believers ([ref:Job 1:6-12|Job 1:6-12]).

Again Satan asks for permission to test Job further, showing the same pattern as in Jesus' words to Simon – Satan wants to test believers, but can only do so within God's allowance ([ref:Job 2:1-6|Job 2:1-6]).

The prophet Amos uses the image of sifting grain as a picture of God's testing and judgment. Jesus' use of the phrase "sift like wheat" has a similar background in Old Testament imagery ([ref:Am 4:11|Amos 4:11]).

The Lord says he will "sift the house of Israel among all nations, as grain is sifted in a sieve". This is the closest Old Testament parallel to Jesus' words about sifting like wheat ([ref:Am 9:9|Amos 9:9]).

Satan rises up against Israel and incites David to count the people. This shows Satan's role as accuser and tempter of God's people, reflecting his desire to sift the disciples ([ref:1 Krøn 21:1|1 Chronicles 21:1]).

Satan stands as accuser against the high priest Joshua, but the Lord rebukes Satan. This scene illustrates Satan's role as accuser of believers, just as Jesus here warns Peter about Satan's attacks ([ref:Sak 3:1-2|Zechariah 3:1-2]).

Peter, who himself experienced Satan's sifting, later warns that the devil goes around like a roaring lion seeking someone to devour. His personal experience from this moment shapes his exhortation ([ref:1 Pet 5:8|1 Peter 5:8]).

Jesus' words continue with him saying he has prayed for Simon that his faith may not fail, and that when he turns back, he should strengthen his brothers. This intercession is the answer to Satan's demand ([ref:Luk 22:32|Luke 22:32]).

In his high priestly prayer, Jesus asks the Father to keep the disciples from the evil one, not that they be taken out of the world. This shows Jesus' intercession for the disciples against Satan's attacks ([ref:Joh 17:15|John 17:15]).

Paul exhorts believers to put on the full armor of God so they can stand against the devil's cunning schemes. Satan's desire to sift the disciples illustrates exactly the spiritual battle Paul describes ([ref:Ef 6:11-12|Ephesians 6:11-12]).

Peter's denial of Jesus fulfills the warning given in this verse. Satan was allowed to sift Peter, and Peter fell – but he was restored in line with Jesus' intercession ([ref:Luk 22:54-62|Luke 22:54-62]).
